title: Lazarus Raised and the Call to Rejoice
english: …this: that He will raise even the foreign nations. Here, then, are three different kinds of the dead. But when He raised Lazarus from the tomb, four days dead, a man made up of the four elements, who already stank (John 11:39), who had decayed, who had been mastered by worms, it was made known to the rulers and authorities in heaven and to those on earth (Ephesians 3:10) that He will raise all humanity, made up of the four elements, even if it has stunk in the sin of the transgression, even if it has rotted in the impiety of idolatry, even if, as by worms, it has been mastered by demons and taken captive to do their will (2 Timothy 2:26).

When they saw this, the angels in secret and human beings openly were astonished and amazed, and they began to cry out and say: “Hosanna in the highest! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!” (Matthew 21:9). They praised Him not only as a worker of signs, but also as the King who took captive the whole captivity that the devil and death had held captive since time began (Psalm 68:18; Ephesians 4:8). For these reasons and others like them, the divine prophets proclaim Him King.

Now the prophets we have named are hosts who feed rational souls. As the months of the year, each in its turn, feed human bodies, so they too, each in turn, or rather all together, feed the souls of the faithful at each feast and at all times, and they make Christians drunk with divine teachings, as one of them says somewhere: “They will be drunk with the richness of Your house” (Psalm 36:8).

Come, then, all who love the kingdom of the Lord, let us listen, and they will tell us what the great Zechariah, glorious among the prophets, prophesies to us about it. Let us understand the good news the herald announces as he runs ahead of the kingdom long before its time. Come, as rational guests, let us enjoy the words that come from the mouth of God through Zechariah, our spiritual host; for it has fallen to him to feed us at this feast, as the Lord says: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).

Since sorrow is hateful to people and joy is longed for, he begins his cry with joy, saying: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion” (Zechariah 9:9). “Rejoice greatly,” the prophet cries to those in captivity. “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). Why “Rejoice”? And why “greatly,” and “be glad and delight” (Zechariah 2:10)? Because He who brings you back has come, as the father of the King who brings you back foretold, saying: “When the Lord brought back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted; then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with gladness” (Psalm 126:1–2).

“Rejoice,” he says, because you are returning from captivity to the demons and from exile in this age to the Jerusalem above (Galatians 4:26), which your father Abraham awaited (Hebrews 11:10), as the blessed apostle Paul says somewhere: “But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, to the festal gathering and church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the Judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect” (Hebrews 12:22–23). That is the place from which “pain, sorrow, and sighing have fled away” (Isaiah 35:10), where all the righteous dwell and rejoice. Then it is “be glad and delight” (Zechariah 2:10) and “rejoice greatly, O daughter,” plainly the daughter of this Zion.

“And why,” she asks, “should I rejoice greatly, O prophet?” “Rejoice,” because that dreadful one will no longer take you captive; and “greatly,” because the One who rescues you is not like the other kings: He is an eternal King, and His kingdom is eternal, as the angel Gabriel says to His mother, the Virgin Mary: “And of His kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33). And as His kingdom is eternal, so your salvation is eternal. That is why he says: “Rejoice greatly; proclaim, O daughter of Jerusalem” (Zechariah 9:9).

“What shall I proclaim, O prophet?” Proclaim thanksgiving, praise, and hymns to your King, who came down from the heights of heaven to save you. Proclaim: “Hosanna in the highest, from where You came to save me; blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21:9).

And look with me at the evangelist, how he proclaims Christ as twofold. When he says, “Hosanna in the highest,” he shows the exalted nature of the Godhead; and when he says, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord,” he signifies the substance of His humanity, the blessed seed with which blessed Abraham was blessed, that in his seed all the nations of the earth should be blessed (Genesis 22:18). For he says: “Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father…” (Mark 11:10)
translator_notes: The section opens in the middle of the sentence begun at the end of the previous section, and ends in the middle of Mark 11:10, which the next section completes.
The “three different kinds of the dead” are the widow’s son, the synagogue ruler’s daughter, and the centurion’s servant, named at the end of the previous section.
Psalm 126:1 is quoted as the Septuagint has it: “like those who are comforted”, where the Hebrew reads “like those who dream”. Hesychius ascribes the Psalm to David, “the father of the King”.
Psalm numbers follow the English Bible. In the Septuagint, Psalm 68:18 is 67:19, Psalm 36:8 is 35:9, and Psalm 126:1–2 is 125:1–2. Zechariah 2:10 is 2:14 in the Septuagint.

title: Daughter of Zion and the Colt Set Free
english: …David” (Mark 11:10).

Let us take up the earlier saying again and press it like a prophetic breast, for it still has good things to give, milk and contemplation. For he says: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; proclaim, O daughter of Jerusalem” (Zechariah 9:9). And why “daughter of Zion” and not “Zion,” and “daughter of Jerusalem” and not “Jerusalem”? Listen with understanding, I beg you.

Just as plants, birds, four-footed beasts, and human beings have their names according to the difference of their form and power, so each stroke of the divine oracles has its own power and its own spiritual sense. So let us search out why the prophet calls the Jerusalem that now believes first “daughter of Zion” and then “daughter of Jerusalem.” For he says: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; proclaim, O daughter of Jerusalem” (Zechariah 9:9).

“Zion” means “thirsting.” She is the assembly of the righteous and the prophets who, from the beginning until the coming of Christ, thirsted to be united to the divine and worshipful substance of the Godhead and to be pleasing to it, as Peter, the chief of the apostles, says: “that they may become partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4). These, as they sought the Lord and thirsted for Him, were called Zion, as one of them said: “My soul has thirsted for God, the mighty, the living One” (Psalm 42:2).

But when they attained and drew near, or rather, appeared before Him and beheld His face (for so another version reads), they became Jerusalem, “seeing God and a watchtower of all knowledge.” He calls the faithful in the Lord the daughter of this Zion: those who thirst through faith and, by doing the commandments of the Gospel, seek to find the Lord who is hidden in them, as the Holy Spirit says: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob” (Psalm 24:6). And when they attain Him, they are called the daughter of the Jerusalem we have named, for they behold God and look out over spiritual knowledge.

The prophet, begging God through the Spirit to show forth such a Zion and Jerusalem, says: “Remember Your congregation, which You acquired from the beginning” (Psalm 74:2). So, together with Zion, this mother of yours: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; proclaim, O daughter of Jerusalem” (Zechariah 9:9), and cry out in heavenly fashion with your mother: “Hosanna in the highest, blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21:9).

And what does the Gospel say? “When they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage” (Matthew 21:1). For He was coming to the upper room so that the faithful might eat Him, “to the Mount of Olives” (Matthew 21:1), which is the faithful church from the people. “Then Jesus sent two of His disciples” (Matthew 21:1), who are the two choirs of the prophets and the apostles. For when the apostles made disciples of the nations (Matthew 28:19), they had with them the God-inspired oracles of the prophets, which bear witness to Christ, just as Ezekiel, great among the prophets, saw them: “a wheel,” he says, “within a wheel” (Ezekiel 1:16), flying and running.

Jesus says to them: “Go into the village opposite you” (Matthew 21:2); for He sent them into the whole inhabited world of the nations, because until then the nations stood opposed to the faithful church from the people. He sent them at the fitting time “into the village opposite,” the village of the nations, for it was ready to receive the two choirs of apostles and prophets already named.

They were sent “to bring the colt to Him” (Luke 19:35), and the colt is the nations, so that He might mount them and reign over them, as the psalmist says: “God has become King over the nations; the Lord sits on His holy throne” (Psalm 47:8). “On which no one has ever sat” (Mark 11:2; Luke 19:30): for the nations had neither God mounting and ruling over them, nor law, nor prophets. “Untie it,” He says, “and bring it to Me” (Matthew 21:2; Luke 19:30). For the apostles untied the nations from darkness, that is, from ignorance of God; from error, from sin, from slavery to an alien master, from “the power of darkness” (Colossians 1:13), from “the ruler of this age” (John 12:31). And they brought them to the Lord, their Creator and Maker.

And see, He sits on them and reigns as upon the cherubim (Psalm 99:1), while they cry out and say: “Hosanna in the highest, blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven and glory in the highest” (Matthew 21:9; Luke 19:38), for so Luke puts it. Why does he say, “Peace in heaven”? Did the angels not have peace in heaven? Yes, they certainly had peace among themselves, “the peace that surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4:7), as the most wise Paul says. They had peace in heaven, but they did not have it with human beings; heaven, then, kept its peace to itself. But when the…
translator_notes: The section opens with the last word of Mark 11:10 (“David”), and ends in the middle of a sentence that the next section completes.
“Each stroke” is the small stroke of a written letter; the phrase may echo Matthew 5:18, but the echo is not certain, so it is not cited in the text.

“Zion” as “thirsting” and Jerusalem as “seeing God” are traditional explanations of the names. The words in quotation marks after “they became Jerusalem” come from such an explanation, not from Scripture.
“Another version” is probably another Greek translation of the Psalm, which reads “appear before Him” and “behold His face” (Psalm 42:2).
Bethphage: Hesychius links the name with the Greek word for “eat” (“so that the faithful might eat Him”). The play cannot be carried into English.
“The ruler of this age” is cited to John 12:31 for its sense (the devil); the wording also echoes 1 Corinthians 2:6.
Psalm numbers follow the English Bible. In the Septuagint, Psalm 42:2 is 41:3, Psalm 24:6 is 23:6, Psalm 74:2 is 73:2, Psalm 47:8 is 46:9, and Psalm 99:1 is 98:1.

title: Garments, Palms, and the Humble King
english: …angels saw all humanity being raised through the sign of Lazarus, and the nations being untied like the colt and coming to be ruled by their Creator, then heaven too was at peace with human beings, and with one accord they cried out and said: “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven and glory in the highest” (Luke 19:38).

“And they put the garments on the colt” (Matthew 21:7): these signify the grace He gave them among the nations, and through this grace “they set Jesus on them” (Luke 19:35). And not only through grace, but also through their own virtues, as the evangelist signifies when he says: “And others spread their garments on the road” (Luke 19:36). By this he hints at their own virtues, which they yoked to grace, as the inspired Paul says plainly: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we boast in hope of the glory of God” (Romans 5:1–2).

That much concerns grace. “And not only this, but we also boast in our afflictions, knowing that affliction produces endurance, and endurance proven character, and proven character hope; and hope does not put us to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:3–5).

And “they spread them on the ground” means that their virtues were seen bodily, openly, and by the senses before the nations, as the apostle also says elsewhere on this point: “What you have seen in me, and heard, and received, these things do” (Philippians 4:9). But let us return to our subject.

“The crowds that went before Him and those that followed cried out” (Matthew 21:9) with praises and with olive branches, which signify the practical work of the outer man, and with palm fronds, which point to the spiritual, contemplative, and pure work of the inner man. “They cried out, saying: Hosanna in the highest” (Matthew 21:9). For in truth all the crowds of the righteous, the prophets, and the priests, who are those who go before and those who follow, cry out in faith and say: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest” (Matthew 21:9).

As the evangelist says: “All this took place to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet, saying: Say to the daughter of Zion” (Matthew 21:4–5). To whom do you say “Say,” O prophet? Look, you proclaim it yourself; you say it yourself. “I,” he says, “longed to see and to hear, and not I alone, but many prophets and righteous men as well” (Matthew 13:17). But I speak also to those who are present and are made disciples, who see and hear the King of Zion, so that they may say and proclaim: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your King is coming to you” (Matthew 21:5).

And he did not say simply “is coming,” but “is coming to you,” that is, to become yours and to dwell in you. “Behold, your King is coming to you, righteous and saving” (Zechariah 9:9), saving from slavery to the enemy those who believe in Him.

“Gentle, and mounted on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden” (Matthew 21:5), that is, humble-minded, and in His humility “destroying the chariots of the kingdom of Ephraim” (Zechariah 9:10), that is, the kingdom of the devil, who reigned over Israel and over the nations. According to the letter, too, He destroyed the kingdom of the Jewish people; for the anointing and the kingdom of the Jews lasted until Christ, and then ceased. “And the horse,” he says, “from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 9:10), that is, all the pride of their rule, by means of His humble colt.

The patriarch Jacob, blessing Judah and revealing the blessing given to his fathers Abraham and Isaac, which is Christ, says: “Binding his colt to the vine” (Genesis 49:11). For to the vine that was moved out of Egypt and filled the whole land (Psalm 80:8–9) with the teaching of its prophets and righteous men, he bound the unclean nations; for the colt is unclean under the Law, and so are the nations.

“Binding his colt to the vine” (Genesis 49:11). Why? So that they might receive from it the Law and the Prophets and the knowledge of God in them, that is, Christ, who is the blessing and the cleansing of the nations. For he says: “and the foal of his donkey to the tendril” (Genesis 49:11). The tendril, that is, the shoot from the vine, is Christ, who sprang from the vine of the synagogue that came out of Egypt, as Jacob himself says to him: “From a shoot…” (Genesis 49:9)

translator_notes: The section opens in the middle of the sentence begun at the end of the previous section, and ends in the middle of Genesis 49:9, which the next section completes.
The edition puts two phrases in square brackets as not part of the text: “and palm branches” after the olive branches, and “and practical” before “contemplative”. They are left out.
Hesychius has the prophet speak Christ’s words about the prophets and righteous men who longed to see and hear (Matthew 13:17).
“From a shoot” is Genesis 49:9 in the Septuagint: “From a shoot, my son, you went up.”
Psalm 80:8–9 is Psalm 79:9–10 in the Septuagint.
